title: New Cholesterol Guideline: 6 Updates to Keep on Your Radar
summary: The 2026 cholesterol guideline adds 30-year risk, LDL targets and universal Lp(a) testing. Alison Megliola, RD, explains what changed and why it matters.
body_markdown:
September 24, 2026


# New Cholesterol Guideline: 6 Updates to Keep on Your Radar


By


[Alison Megliola, MS, RD, CDCES](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alisonmegliola)


This edition covers:


- Why the cholesterol guideline has changed


- How these changes impact clinical practice and patient care


- The importance of fostering cholesterol awareness at the population level


Progress against heart disease has stalled. Cardiovascular disease still kills more Americans than any other cause, and the American Heart Association's (AHA)


[2026 statistics update](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/heart-disease-stroke-deaths-down-yet-still-kill-more-in-u-s-than-any-other-cause)


shows nearly half of US adults now live with some form of it.


As a response, in spring 2026, eleven medical societies led by the American College of Cardiology and AHA retired the


[2018 Blood Cholesterol Guideline](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000624)


and released a new


[2026 Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001423)


. The rename is not cosmetic, it signals a real shift in how cardiovascular health is measured, when treatment starts, and which labs to prioritize.


But that shift won’t move the needle on heart disease immediately; medical guidelines always change faster than in practice.


Research suggests it takes an


[average of 17 years](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3241518/)


for new evidence to reach routine care, and cholesterol is a textbook case: a silent condition, competing for minutes in a short PCP or specialist visit, with lab work and follow-ups stretched across months. This is why most patients are still being managed against older clinical standards. And it’s not because their doctor isn't trying, but because change at this scale takes time to work its way into every exam room, and doctor’s visits are often very brief. That’s why it’s important for both healthcare providers, and those who provide health coverage, to stay current on the new guideline.


When it comes to sharing new and relevant health guidelines, the responsibility doesn’t sit solely with care providers either. Employers provide the lion’s share of health coverage for working Americans, and should play a role in understanding and informing their populations.


Employers who learn the new cholesterol standards can set expectations with payers on care benchmarks and support, and advocate for the coverage that closes that gap.


Patients who understand the new guideline can walk into a visit knowing whether their low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is at goal, whether they need a lipoprotein(a) \[Lp(a)\] test, and what their 30-year risk looks like. However, most patients


[are not equipped with the knowledge.](https://www.powershealth.org/about-us/newsroom/health-library/2026/02/02/survey-finds-gaps-in-americans-knowledge-of-unhealthy-cholesterol#:~:text=The%20survey%20revealed%20that,looks%20for%20clogged%20arteries.)


## LDL is Still the Priority With Several Major Updates


The cholesterol guideline is like a blueprint doctors use to decide which labs to order, when to prescribe medication, and what "at goal" means for each patient. When that manual is rewritten, the aforementioned items should change too.


The 2018 guideline was built around LDL cholesterol, statin intensity, and a 10-year risk estimate of heart attack or stroke. The 2026 version keeps LDL at the center but adds six practice-changing updates that patients should expect to see reflected in the labs their doctor orders and the goals they discuss:


1. **Risk assessment now looks 30 years out and factors in kidney and metabolic health** . The 2018 guideline used a calculator called the Pooled Cohort Equations that estimated a patient’s 10-year risk of a heart attack or stroke. The 2026 guideline replaces risk assessment with a newer, more contemporary tool called


[PREVENT](https://professional.heart.org/en/guidelines-and-statements/prevent-calculator)


. This new tool estimates both 10-year and 30-year risk of the same events and folds in kidney function and metabolic health.


2. **Consider therapy at a lower risk level.** The 2018 threshold was a 10-year risk of 7.5% — roughly a 1-in-13 chance of a heart attack or stroke over the next decade. The 2026 guideline moves that threshold down: it


*is*


*reasonable* to consider statin therapy at 3-5% risk and


*is recommended* at >5% risk.


3. **Absolute LDL goals are set** . The 2018 guideline steered clear of naming specific LDL numbers, instead asking clinicians to aim for a ≥50% reduction from baseline in high-risk patients and 30–49% in moderate-risk patients. The 2026 guideline puts numeric targets back on the table: LDL <55 mg/dL for members at very high risk (typically those who have already had a cardiovascular event) and <70 mg/dL for most others on treatment, with less aggressive goals for lower-risk adults.


4. **Universal Lp(a) testing** . Every adult should have Lp(a) measured at least once. Lp(a) is a cholesterol-carrying lipoprotein in the blood that is genetically determined and stable across life–and unlikely to change. This single test reveals whether someone carries an inherited source of cardiovascular risk that would otherwise go unseen. This is brand-new to the 2026 guideline.


5. **ApoB gets an operational role.** Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) is a structural protein found on fat particles in the blood. The American Heart Association (AHA) describes ApoB as


[the number of cars on a freeway](https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/cholesterol/how-to-get-your-cholesterol-tested/apolipoprotein-b)


vs. how many passengers are inside each car, i.e. LDL. The more traffic on the freeway, the higher the risk. Once a patient’s LDL is at goal, the ApoB number helps guide therapy, particularly in members with elevated triglycerides, diabetes, or a low-achieved LDL. Low-achieved LDL means someone whose LDL is already well-controlled on treatment (the ideal number of passengers in each car); at that point, a standard lipid panel without ApOB can miss residual risk carried by other atherogenic, i.e. plaque-building, particles.


6. **Supplements are out** . The 2018 guideline was silent on dietary supplements. The 2026 guideline takes a stance on supplements for the first time, and advises against them for lowering LDL or triglycerides, including fish oil, red yeast rice, garlic, turmeric, cinnamon, and plant sterols. In the


[SPORT trial](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2022.10.013)


, no supplement outperformed a placebo, whereas a low-dose statin cut LDL by 38%.


[Given that ~73% of adults with ASCVD take at least one supplement](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.123.033748)


, this is a real shift in public perception.


## Two Labs that Could Reshape Prevention


Earlier this year, my colleague Justin Wu, MD flagged in


[Meet the New Heart Health Tech Stack](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/meet-new-heart-health-tech-stack-ai-cuffless-monitors-behavior-g1aif)


that biomarkers like Lp(a) and ApoB were entering risk assessment standards. The 2026 guideline formalized that shift.


- **Lp(a):** As mentioned above, this is the risk factor hiding in plain sight. While Lp(a) is genetic and not meaningfully moved by diet or exercise, testing for it triggers earlier, aggressive control of other modifiable factors, including LDL, blood pressure, blood glucose, and lifestyle.


- **ApoB:** Going back to the freeway analogy in the previous section, ApoB is the truer count of atherogenic particles vs. LDL, and often highlights residual cardiovascular risk that standard lipid panels might overlook.


**LDL is still the first target** . Screening, initial goals, and statin decisions still start with LDL.


## Why New Guidelines Don’t Automatically Reach Patients


Guidelines move faster than practice. Even a well-intentioned PCP faces:


- **Time and volume constraints.** Cholesterol competes with dozens of decisions in a short visit, and unlike diabetes or hypertension, it often has no symptoms to warrant a conversation.


- **The lab-to-decision lag.** Cholesterol care often requires a lab draw, a follow-up visit, a treatment decision, and often a 4-12-week recheck, and each step is an opportunity to drop off. For context, compare this care stream with hypertension or diabetes, where a blood pressure cuff or glucose monitor gives instant feedback.


- **The system rarely translates the new standard back to the patient.** Most people never


[see their numbers explained](https://www.omadahealth.com/resource-center/know-your-numbers-how-diabetes-impacts-cholesterol-and-cardiovascular-health)


against the current guideline. So far, most patients are not told to test their Lp(a), and are not shown their 30-year risk. This communication lag in the care system leaves patients without the information they need to advocate for their health.


Because elements of heart disease, like plaque buildup, develop silently, the cost of this knowledge gap doesn't show up in this quarter's claims, it shows up in avoidable events years later.


## How to Foster Cholesterol Awareness in Your Population


Educating people on the new cholesterol guideline can be a powerful catalyst for change. When people understand what "at goal" means, that Lp(a) is a one-time test worth asking for, and that supplements are not a substitute for treatment, they walk into doctor visits with the right questions and stay engaged between them. That is how a guideline update translates into fewer heart attacks, fewer strokes, and a real bend in the curve of chronic disease. Doing this at population scale requires three things the office visits and followup care are not built to do:


1. **Communicate the guideline simply:** When patients get a lipid panel back, they should see what their numbers mean against the current standard, determine the right numbers were measured, and know which questions to bring to their PCP.


2. **Reinforce daily heart-health behaviors:** Nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and medication adherence that influence LDL and ApoB.


3. **Day-to-day guidance between visits:** Health coaches and technology can extend heart health education into daily life by providing nutrition and exercise guidance, progress tracking, help understanding labs and more.


The 2026 guideline sets a higher bar for what "good" cholesterol care looks like, and primary care will get there eventually. In the meantime, patients and care providers (including employers and payers), can turn toward virtual between-visit care to fill those critical gaps. With more frequent care touch points and dedicated experts, new care standards can reach patients faster.
